title: SQL injection
starter: A website login box passes whatever you type straight into a database query. Suggest what could go wrong, and who might take advantage of it.
starterAnswer: Accept any sensible attempt: this is a hook, not an assessment.
Look for the vocabulary from the lesson objectives appearing in students' own words.
Students who are stuck should still write something: the experience will correct it.
starterNote: Take two or three answers, then leave it open. Come back to it in the plenary, when they can answer it properly.

stations.name: Databases and SQL
facts: Websites store usernames, passwords and records in a database.
SQL (Structured Query Language) is used to ask the database for records, and to add, change or delete them.
SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = 'Sam' asks for Sam's record.
stations.challenge: Write in your own words what SQL is used for.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Websites store usernames, passwords and records in a database.
Also credit: SQL (Structured Query Language) is used to ask the database for records, and to add, change or delete them.

questions.a: Asking a database for records, and adding, changing or deleting them

questions.q: Which part of a website would use SQL?
questions.a: The login page checking a username and password

stations.name: The dangerous line
facts: The code in your starter joins the user's input onto the query as text.
Joining a string to a variable like this is called concatenation.
Whatever the user types becomes part of the SQL command.
stations.challenge: Which line of the starter code is the dangerous one, and why?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: The code in your starter joins the user's input onto the query as text.
Also credit: Joining a string to a variable like this is called concatenation.

questions.q: Joining a string to a variable, as in 'uname = ' + username, is known as what?
Why is building a query this way dangerous?
questions.a: Anything the user types becomes part of the SQL command

stations.name: The attack
facts: An attacker types SQL into the text box instead of a username.
Entering ' OR 1=1 -- makes the condition always true and comments out the rest.
The database returns every record, and the attacker is logged in.
stations.challenge: Explain how typing ' OR 1=1 -- into a login box can work.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: An attacker types SQL into the text box instead of a username.
Also credit: Entering ' OR 1=1 -- makes the condition always true and comments out the rest.

questions.q: What does ' OR 1=1 do inside a query?
questions.a: It makes the condition always true, so every record matches
It turns the rest of the line into a comment, so it is ignored

stations.name: What attackers gain
facts: Log in as another user, including an administrator.
Read every record: names, emails, passwords and card details.
Change or delete records, or even destroy whole tables.
stations.challenge: What could an attacker do with a school's student database?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Log in as another user, including an administrator.
Also credit: Read every record: names, emails, passwords and card details.

questions.q: What can a successful SQL injection attack achieve? Select all that apply.
questions.a: Bypass a login and enter as another user; Read personal data from the database; Change or delete records

stations.name: Stopping injection
facts: Validate input: check it matches what's expected, such as letters and numbers only.
Sanitise input: remove or escape dangerous characters like quotation marks.
Use parameterised queries, which keep the user's input separate from the SQL command.
Give the website's database account only the permissions it needs.
stations.challenge: Which defence is the strongest, and why?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Validate input: check it matches what's expected, such as letters and numbers only.
Also credit: Sanitise input: remove or escape dangerous characters like quotation marks.

questions.q: Which is the strongest defence against SQL injection?
questions.a: Using parameterised queries, so input is never treated as code
Removing or escaping characters that could change the meaning of the query

stations.name: Testing for holes
facts: Penetration testers deliberately try injection attacks to find weaknesses.
Detailed error messages help attackers, so live sites should hide them.
Old, unpatched website software is a common way in.
stations.challenge: Why should a live website never show detailed database errors?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Penetration testers deliberately try injection attacks to find weaknesses.
Also credit: Detailed error messages help attackers, so live sites should hide them.

questions.q: Why do companies pay penetration testers?
questions.a: To find weaknesses like SQL injection before criminals do

questions.q: Why hide detailed error messages on a live site?
questions.a: They can tell an attacker how the database is built

final.name: Final challenge: secure the login

questions.q: Is each practice safe or risky when writing a login page?
questions.a: Building the query by joining text to the user's input = Risky; Using parameterised queries = Safe; Checking input contains only letters and numbers = Safe; Showing the full database error on the page = Risky; Giving the website's database account full admin rights = Risky; Removing or escaping quotation marks in input = Safe; Having the site penetration tested = Safe; Trusting that users will only type a username = Risky

final.note: Students should have predicted these on the worksheet before tapping the star. Mark the prediction, not just the final answer.

exam.q: Describe what happens during an SQL injection attack.
points: Penetration testers deliberately try injection attacks to find weaknesses.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark per point, to a maximum of 3.

exam.q: Explain two techniques a programmer can use to prevent SQL injection.
points: Penetration testers deliberately try injection attacks to find weaknesses.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark per point, to a maximum of 4.

common: Naming a term without saying what it does: most questions need the term and its purpose.
Answering 'it's faster' or 'it's better' with no reason: link it to the characteristic the question is about.
Repeating the question in the answer and stopping there.
